prompt: Put the states of a defect that is fixed first time in order.
trap: Verified before ready for retest would mean the tester checked a build that had not reached them.

prompt: Why is "ready for retest" a state of its own, separate from "fixed"?
hint: Where is the fix in each state?

choices.text: So the developer can test the fix twice
choices.why: The developer tests in "fixed"; this state is about the tester.

choices.text: It says a build with the fix has reached the test environment
choices.why: Right: a fix on the developer's machine cannot be retested yet.

choices.text: Trackers need an even number of states for their boards
choices.why: Nothing about states depends on how a board draws them.

choices.text: It marks the moment the product owner approves the fix
choices.why: Approval of a fix is the retest's job, done by the tester, not the owner.

prompt: Release 1.1 fixed lesson 5's member discount, and students stopped paying half. What happens to the reports?
hint: Does the member discount still fail?

choices.text: Reopen lesson 5's report, since its fix caused the failure
choices.why: Its own retest passes: a member booking five gets 15%. Reopening it would record a false failure.

choices.text: A new report; lesson 5's stays closed
choices.why: Right: a different rule failed, so the student price is a new defect, linked to 1.1's change.

choices.text: Both are closed until release 1.2 ships with the fixes
choices.why: The student price is open and critical; closing it hides it.

choices.text: Lesson 5's report is marked duplicate of the student one
choices.why: They are two rules with two causes, so neither duplicates the other.

prompt: Match each end to what it says about the report.
hint: Three exits at triage, and the normal end.

pairs.right: Already reported; linked to the original
Not a defect, with the reason written on it
A defect the team decided not to fix in this release

right_distractors: Fixed by the developer and closed by the developer

prompt: A developer under pressure marks his own fix "closed" to clear the board. Which check has been skipped?
hint: Who reads the report besides the developer?

choices.text: The triage, which should have set a priority first
choices.why: The triage happened before the work began; the gap is at the other end.

choices.text: None, if the developer tested the change on his own machine
choices.why: His test runs his reading of the report on his machine, which is exactly what a retest is there to question.

choices.text: The retest by somebody else, on the delivered build
choices.why: Right: the one check that does not depend on the developer's own reading.

choices.text: The code review of the change by a second developer
choices.why: A review is useful and separate; the lifecycle's missing step is the retest.

prompt: What does a triage meeting produce?

choices.text: Fixes for the most serious defects, worked out together
choices.why: A triage that debugs runs out of time with half the list undecided.

choices.text: A decision per new report, an order for the open
choices.why: Right: state, priority, a name, and a reason where one is needed.

choices.text: A count of the defects found per tester this week
choices.why: That is a number section 05 calls theatre.

choices.text: The test cases for the next release
choices.why: Cases come from requirements and risks, lesson 2; triage handles reports.

prompt: Order the questions triage asks of a new report, stopping at the first that ends it.
trap: Setting a priority before asking whether it is a defect at all spends the meeting on reports that will be rejected.

prompt: At boxoffice's triage, who owns the priority and who owns the severity?
hint: One knows the business; one knows the reports.

choices.text: Rui owns both, since he will do the work
choices.why: Rui knows the cost of each fix, which informs priority without owning it.

choices.text: Ana owns both, since she filed the reports
choices.why: She proposes a priority; the business cost belongs to the manager.

choices.text: Manager: priority. Ana: severity.
choices.why: Right: the cost to the business against the harm in the product.

choices.text: The manager owns severity; Rui owns priority
choices.why: The other way round from what each of them knows.

prompt: The refund after the show started is major, yet the manager made it P1 beside the critical used-order refund. What justified it?

choices.text: Major defects are P1 whenever a critical one is
choices.why: Priority is not derived from severity; the traceback is major and P2.

choices.text: Rui fixes both in the same lines of code, so together they cost little more
choices.why: Right: priority can follow the cost of the fix as well as the cost of the defect.

choices.text: It is a duplicate of the used-order refund
choices.why: R6 states two conditions; fixing one leaves the other open.

choices.text: Ana raised its severity to critical during the meeting
choices.why: The table keeps it major; nothing new was learnt about the harm.

prompt: What is this lesson's test for whether a new report duplicates an old one?
hint: Think about the fix, not the text.

choices.text: Whether the two titles share most of their words
choices.why: Two duplicates can share no words, like payed and useed; two distinct defects can share many.

choices.text: Whether fixing the first would fix the second
choices.why: Right: the same cause, whatever the words.

choices.text: Whether both happen on the same page of the application
choices.why: The two refund defects share a page and are two causes.

choices.text: Whether the same tester filed both
choices.why: Who filed them says nothing about their cause.

prompt: "A used order can be refunded" and "a refund is accepted after the show started": why are they two reports?
hint: Fix the first and look at the second.

choices.text: They were found in different lessons, by different techniques
choices.why: Where a defect was found does not decide whether it is the same one.

choices.text: One of them is critical and the other one is only major
choices.why: Severity follows from the defects; it does not decide whether they are one.

choices.text: One is on the order page and the other on the booking page
choices.why: Both are on the order page and both answer "Order is now refunded."

choices.text: Refusing used orders leaves the time rule open
choices.why: Right: R6 has two conditions, so two causes, two fixes and two retests.

prompt: A member booking five gets 15% on 1.1, and a report asks for 25%. It is rejected because R5 says discounts do not add up: the ___ one applies.
Three careful testers file the same "should be 25%" report in a month. What does that suggest, beyond the rejection?
hint: Where else can a defect live?

choices.text: R5 reads two ways, which is a defect in the document
choices.why: Right: the response is to reword R5 with the manager, which lesson 6 calls verification.

choices.text: The program is wrong after all and the rejection should be reversed
choices.why: The program does what R5 says; the trouble is in how R5 is read.

choices.text: The testers need to be told to search before filing
choices.why: They may well have searched; the repeat says the wording misleads careful people.

choices.text: The rejections should be turned into deferrals so they stop
choices.why: Deferring says "a defect, later", which is false about the program.

prompt: Last quarter a team marked 40 defects fixed, and 6 came back from the retest. What is the reopen rate, in percent?
Why is "defects found per tester" theatre?

choices.text: Testers find too few defects for the number to vary
choices.why: It varies plenty; the trouble is what people do to move it.

choices.text: It rewards splitting one defect into several reports
choices.why: Right: payed and useed filed apart count twice, and the careful tester looks slow.

choices.text: Trackers cannot attribute a report to the person who filed it
choices.why: Every tracker records the reporter; the number is easy to get, which is the danger.

choices.text: Developers find most defects, so testers always look bad
choices.why: Who finds most is not the point; the number rewards the wrong work.

prompt: Management sets a target of zero open defects at release. What does the lesson expect to happen?
hint: What is the cheapest way to hit it?

choices.text: Quality rises, because every defect gets fixed before shipping
choices.why: Some defects are not worth fixing now; the target makes deferring them look like failure.

choices.text: Nothing changes; teams ignore targets they cannot meet
choices.why: People adapt to the measure they are judged by, which is Goodhart's point.

choices.text: Reports get rejected, deferred or never filed to keep the chart at zero
choices.why: Right: the count is improved without improving the product.

choices.text: Testers stop retesting, since a verified defect still counts as open
choices.why: A verified defect is not open; the pressure is on what gets into the tracker at all.

prompt: boxoffice has two fixes so far and neither was reopened. How should that be reported?

choices.text: Reopen rate 0%: fixes are holding perfectly
choices.why: Two is far too few to support a claim about every fix.

choices.text: Give the count, 0 of 2, and draw no conclusion
choices.why: Right: the count with its denominator, and honesty about what so few can say.

choices.text: It should not be reported until there are a hundred fixes
choices.why: The honest count is worth reporting; it is the conclusion that must wait.

choices.text: Reopen rate undefined, because nothing failed
choices.why: The rate is defined, 0 of 2; it just says very little.

prompt: Nobody at triage can reproduce a report. What happens to it next?

choices.text: It is rejected as not a defect
choices.why: Not yet: the reader and the writer may simply be in different environments.

choices.text: It is deferred to the next release
choices.why: Deferring is for a defect the team has seen and chosen to leave.

choices.text: It goes back to its writer with what was tried
choices.why: Right: the writer checks version and starting state, and it closes only if they cannot see it either.

choices.text: It is marked in progress so a developer can investigate
choices.why: In progress means somebody is fixing a defect the team has seen.

prompt: Which of these numbers can only be improved by improving the work? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The age of the oldest open critical defect
choices.why: Yes: only fixing it or deferring it on purpose moves it, and both are visible.

choices.text: The share of fixes that came back from the retest
choices.why: Yes: fewer reopens needs fixes that hold.

choices.text: The number of reports filed this month
choices.why: Splitting reports raises it and not filing lowers it.

choices.text: The total of open defects, with no severity
choices.why: Closing thirty misspellings lowers it while the critical one stays.

prompt: The misspelt messages are trivial. Why does the triage defer them rather than leave them in "new"?

choices.text: A report left in "new" is deleted after a month by most trackers
choices.why: Trackers do not delete old reports; the problem is that nobody decided anything.

choices.text: Deferring is a decision on record; sitting in "new" is none
choices.why: Right: it can be disagreed with, and it comes back when a release is planned.

choices.text: Deferred reports are fixed automatically in the next release
choices.why: They come back to triage; nothing fixes them automatically.

choices.text: Trivial defects cannot stay in "new", by definition
choices.why: Any report starts in "new"; severity does not move it.
